saint.name: St. Benedict of Nursia
saint.summary: The first monks who asked Benedict to be their abbot put poison in his wine. When he blessed the glass, it shattered, and he told them mildly that he had warned them: their way of life and his would never agree. Then he went back to his cave. He had left Rome to be alone with God, yet people kept finding him: a priest at Easter, shepherds, a Gothic king who tested him with a servant in royal robes, and a sister whose prayer brought down a storm to keep him talking all night. How did a hermit who fled the world become the father of monks who live together, and the patron of Europe?
saint.biography:
The Abbot They Tried to Poison

The monks had come to him first. Their abbot had died, and they had heard of a hermit living in a cave near Subiaco, and they wanted him to rule them in the dead man’s place. He said no. Their ways, he told them, were different from his, and the two would never agree. They went on asking, and in the end he gave in.

It went as he had said it would. He held them to the regular life of monks, and they found that they had called in a master who meant it. Before long some of them mixed poison into his wine. When the glass came to him, Benedict made the sign of the cross over it, and the glass broke in pieces, Gregory the Great writes, “as though the sign of the cross had been a stone thrown against it.”

He understood. He did not curse them or call down judgment. With what Gregory calls “a mild countenance and quiet mind,” he spoke to the men who had just tried to kill him:

“Almighty God have mercy upon you, and forgive you: why have you used me in this manner? Did not I tell you before hand, that our manner of living could never agree together?”

— Benedict to the monks who poisoned his wine, in Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book II, chapter 3 (English of 1608)

“Go your ways,” he told them, “and seek ye out some other father suitable to your own conditions.” Then he left them and went back to the wilderness, where, in Gregory’s phrase, he dwelt with himself.

It is a strange beginning for a man whom a pope would one day call the father of Europe. The first community that asked Benedict to be its father would rather kill him than live under him. Yet fourteen centuries later, when Pope Paul VI named him principal patron of all Europe, he called him a messenger of peace, a builder of unity, a teacher of civilization, and the founder of monastic life in the West. The Rule that Benedict wrote for his later monks, which Gregory praised for its discretion, asks them near its end to bear one another’s weaknesses, of body and of character, with the greatest patience.

Between that broken glass and that patient chapter lies the whole of his life, and its question. Benedict went into the wilderness to be alone with God. But people would not leave him alone. A priest was sent to find him on Easter Day, shepherds took him for a wild animal, Roman nobles brought him their sons, a Gothic king came to test him, and his own sister kept him talking through a night of thunder. How did a man who ran from the world into a cave become the father of monks who live together, and the patron of a continent? The story begins in Rome, with a young student who looked at the life around him and, as Gregory puts it, drew back his foot.

Learned Ignorance, Unlearned Wisdom

Benedict came from the province of Nursia, born, Gregory says, “of honourable parentage,” and that is nearly all Gregory says of his family. Later writers gave his parents names and traced the family to a great Roman house, but Gregory, who had his story from men who had lived with Benedict, mentions neither. What Gregory does tell is that even as a boy he had, as it were, an old man’s mind in a young body. He was brought up in Rome and set to study letters, and what he saw there made him turn back.

Around him, other young men were learning the same books and sliding into dissolute lives, and the learning seemed to be carrying them down rather than lifting them. Benedict drew back his foot before he followed them. He left his books, he left his father’s house and its wealth, and he went out of the city. Gregory sums up the young man in a famous line: he went away “instructed with learned ignorance, and furnished with unlearned wisdom.” He had learned enough to know what he did not want.

He did not go entirely alone. His nurse, who loved him tenderly, would not give him up, and she went with him. They stopped at a place the old English translation calls Enside, which is Effide, the modern Affile. There Benedict lived for a while among a company of devout men, at the church of St. Peter.

At Effide a small household disaster struck. The nurse had borrowed a sieve from the neighbors, and it fell and broke in two. It was not hers, and she wept over it. Benedict gathered up the two pieces and, Gregory says, “with tears fell to his prayers.” When he rose, he found the sieve “so whole that the place could not be seen where before it was broken.”

The townspeople heard of it, and they hung the sieve over the door of their church, where it was still hanging, Gregory writes, “even to these very troubles of the Lombards,” that is, into his own day. It is the first wonder Gregory tells of Benedict, and it is a kind one: a young man who had walked away from a fortune prayed with tears over his nurse’s borrowed sieve.

It also spoiled his plan. He had left Rome to escape the world’s applause, and now a whole town was talking about him. So he stole away from Effide, from its admirers and even from his nurse, and went on alone toward a wild place called Subiaco.

Bread on a Rope

Subiaco lay almost forty miles from Rome, where the water of a spring had gathered into a lake. On the road there Benedict met a monk named Romanus, who belonged to a monastery nearby. Romanus kept his secret, gave him the habit of a monk, and became his servant in the strangest way. Benedict settled in a narrow cave, and for three years no one else knew he was there.

Romanus stole what hours he could from his own monastery’s day, and saved what bread he could, and brought it to the hermit. From the top of the high rock above the cave, where no path ran, he let the bread down on a long rope, with a little bell tied on so that the hermit would know when it came. Gregory records that “the old enemy” once threw a stone and broke the bell. It is the first picture of community in Benedict’s life: a monk with a rope above, a young man in a cave below, and one brother quietly keeping another alive.

Three years in a cave is long enough to lose count of the days, and Benedict did. A priest a good way off had made ready a good dinner for himself when the Lord spoke to him in a vision: “Thou hast provided good cheer for thyself, and my servant in such a place is afflicted with hunger.” The priest set out, and on Easter Day he found the hermit in his cave. They prayed together and talked for a while of the things of God. Then the priest said, “Rise up, brother, and let us dine, because to-day is the feast of Easter.” Benedict had not known. His answer is one of the gentlest lines in the whole of Gregory’s book:

“I know that it is Easter with me and a great feast, having found so much favour at God’s hands as this day to enjoy your company.”

— Benedict to the priest who found him in the cave, in Gregory, Dialogues II, chapter 1 (English of 1608)

For a man who had fled to be alone, it is a revealing answer. The feast, for him, was a visitor.

Other visitors followed. Shepherds came upon him dressed in skins, and at first thought he was some beast. When they understood that he was a servant of God, many of them changed their lives, and word of the man in the cave began to spread through the countryside.

The cave did not protect him from himself. One day, Gregory says, a little black bird began to fly about his face. Soon afterward the memory of a woman he had once seen came back to him, and with it a temptation of the flesh. Near the cave grew briers and nettles. He stripped off his clothes, threw himself into them, and rolled there until his body was covered with wounds. “By the wounds of his body,” Gregory writes, “he cured the wounds of his soul.” Benedict told his disciples about it himself, and he told them something else: after that day he never felt such a temptation again.

It is a hard story, and it is his own. The man who would one day write a rule that asks for nothing harsh or heavy had first learned, alone and in pain, how strong the enemy within can be. By now his solitude was ending. People knew where he was. One day a group of monks came to the cave with a request he did not want to grant.

Dwelling With Himself

They were the monks of a neighboring monastery, the ones who would later hand him the poisoned cup. Gregory does not name their house; later tradition placed it at Vicovaro. Their abbot had died, and they wanted the hermit in his place. Benedict refused for a long time, warning them that their manners and his could never agree. When he finally gave in, he did not soften. He saw that the regular life of monks was kept, and they answered him with poison.

Gregory tells all this to his pupil Peter, who listens and asks questions all through the Dialogues, and here he stops to defend Benedict for leaving. A saint may leave a community that cannot be helped, he says; even St. Paul, he points out, was let down from Damascus in a basket. So Benedict went back to his cave and, in the phrase Gregory makes famous, “dwelt with himself,” habitare secum.

It did not last. Men came to the wilderness to live under him, and so many came that he built twelve monasteries, with twelve monks in each, “and a few he kept with himself.” The hermit had become the founder of a small world of monks among the hills around the lake.

Romans of rank began to bring him their sons to be raised in God’s service. A nobleman named Evitius gave him Maurus. A senator named Tertullus brought Placidus, “a boy of tender years.” Both boys will appear again and again in Benedict’s story.

Three of the twelve monasteries stood high on the mountain with no water of their own, and the monks were worn out with carrying it up. One night Benedict climbed the mountain himself with the boy Placidus, prayed there, and laid three stones to mark the place where he had prayed.

The next day he sent the monks up to dig where the three stones lay. They dug, and the rock began “sweating drops of water,” and then a spring broke out that flowed, Gregory says, “even to this day.” The abbot had answered their weariness with a night of prayer they never saw.

The boy who had climbed the mountain with him that night was the next one to need him.

Running Across the Lake

Before that, there was the Goth. Among the men who came to Subiaco was a Goth, a man poor in spirit, as Gregory describes him, and Benedict received him into the community. Benedict set him to work with a billhook, clearing briers from a plot by the edge of the lake. As the Goth worked, the iron head slipped off the handle and fell into the water, into a place “so deep, that there was no hope” of getting it back.

The Goth ran in fear to Maurus and confessed what he had done, and Maurus went to the abbot. Benedict came down to the shore, took the empty handle from the Goth, and put it into the water. The iron rose from the bottom of the lake. Benedict handed the billhook back with a sentence that holds much of his character:

“Behold here is thy bill again, work on, and be sad no more.”

Peter, when he heard it, thought of the prophet Elisha and his axe-head. But the tone of the story is Benedict’s own: no lecture on carelessness, no penance, only the tool returned and the work resumed and the sadness lifted.

Then came the day Placidus went down to the lake and fell in. The water caught him and carried him out from the shore “so far as one may shoot an arrow.” Benedict was in his cell, but he knew at once. He called Maurus and sent him running. Maurus ran down to the water and did not stop at the edge. He ran on across the surface of the lake, seized Placidus by the hair, and dragged him back to the shore.

When it was over, no one would take credit for it. Benedict said the wonder came from Maurus’s obedience. Maurus insisted it came from the abbot’s command; he had only done as he was told. It was Placidus, the one who had been in the water, who settled the matter. While he was being pulled out, he said, he had seen “the Abbot’s garment upon his head.”

Each man insisted the wonder belonged to the other, and it took the boy who had nearly drowned to decide it. At Subiaco, it seems, no one wanted the credit.

Not everyone who watched it grow was glad.

The Crow and the Poisoned Loaf

Not far from Subiaco stood a church whose priest was named Florentius. Gregory pauses to tell Peter that this man was the grandfather of “Florentius our sub-deacon,” a cleric Gregory knew, so the story came close to home. The priest envied Benedict. The abbot’s monasteries were full, his name was spreading, and the priest nearby could not bear it.

Florentius sent Benedict a loaf of bread, and the bread was poisoned. Benedict knew. Every day at dinner a crow came to him from the nearby wood and took bread from his hand, and when it came that day, he threw it the poisoned loaf and gave it an order:

“In the name of Jesus Christ our Lord, take up that loaf, and leave it in some such place where no man may find it.”

— Benedict to the crow, in Gregory, Dialogues II, chapter 8 (English of 1608)

The crow did not like the errand. It opened its mouth and spread its wings and hopped about the loaf, crying out as though it wished to obey and could not. Benedict told it again and again to take the loaf up without fear. At last, “with much ado,” it took the loaf and flew away. Three hours later it was back, and took its usual bread from Benedict’s hand. A man had tried to murder him, and Benedict had answered with an errand for a bird.

Florentius tried again, and this time he aimed at the monks. He sent seven naked young women into the yard of the monastery to dance in front of the young brothers. Benedict, “fearing the danger” for his disciples, decided that he would be the one to go. He “gave place to envy,” Gregory says. He appointed governors for the monasteries he had built there, and with a few monks he left Subiaco.

Benedict was “scarce ten miles off” when word reached him from Maurus. Florentius was dead: the room where he was had collapsed and killed him. Maurus was glad of the news. Benedict was not. He mourned the man who had tried to poison him and to corrupt his young monks, and he gave Maurus a penance for rejoicing at an enemy’s death.

Peter, hearing all this, was reminded of Moses, of Elisha, of St. Peter, of Elijah, and of David. But the most telling moment belongs to no prophet. It is the abbot, ten miles down the road, sorrowing for the man who had driven him out.

He did not go back. With his few monks he went on to a mountain above a town called Cassino, and there he began again.

Fire on Apollo’s Mountain

“The town, which is called Cassino,” Gregory writes, “standeth upon the side of an high mountain.” There stood an ancient chapel where the country people still worshipped the god Apollo, with woods around it. Benedict beat the idol in pieces, overthrew the altar, and set fire to the woods. Inside the old temple he built an oratory dedicated to St. Martin, and on the very spot where Apollo’s altar had stood he built an oratory of St. John the Baptist. Then he went out and preached to the people of the countryside around.

That second oratory, raised where the altar of Apollo had been, will come back at the end of his story.

The old enemy, Gregory says, did not give up the mountain quietly. He began to appear to Benedict openly, in a form Benedict could see. The monks saw nothing, but they heard the voice. First it called him by name: “Blessed Bennet.” The old English calls him Bennet, and his Latin name, Benedictus, means blessed. Then the voice turned: “Cursed Bennet, and not blessed: what hast thou to do with me?”

The building of the monastery went on under this pressure, and Gregory tells a string of stories from those years. A great stone that the monks needed would not move until Benedict came and blessed it; the monks decided that the devil was sitting on it. When the monks dug up a brass idol, the kitchen suddenly seemed to be on fire, though the fire turned out to be only a phantom.

The worst came while a new wall was going up. The devil, Gregory says, threw it down, and it fell on a young monk, the son of a courtier. So badly had the stones broken his limbs and his very bones that his brothers brought him to the abbot in a sack. Benedict took him into his cell and prayed alone. In the very same hour the young monk was sound again, and Benedict sent him back to work on the wall.

The monks of Cassino were learning that their abbot saw more than they did. They were about to learn that he saw more than they wished.

Nothing Hidden From the Abbot

The rule of the house was that monks who went out did not eat outside the monastery. One day some brothers who had been out ate at the house of a devout woman. When they came home, Benedict asked where they had eaten. Nowhere, they told him. He answered, “Why do you tell an untruth? for did you not go into such a woman’s house? and eat such and such kind of meat, and drink so many cups?”

Gregory had a story of the same kind about the brother of Valentinian, one of his four witnesses. This brother was a layman who would not eat on his way to the abbey until he got there. Once he ate on the road, and when he arrived, Benedict told him so.

Some of the stories are funny. A lay brother named Exhilaratus, a man of Gregory’s own circle (“whom you know,” Gregory reminds Peter), once hid a flagon of wine in a bush. The abbot warned him: “Take heed, my son, that thou drinkest not of that flagon which thou hast hidden in the bush: but first be careful to bow it down, and thou shalt find what is within it.” Exhilaratus tipped the flagon over, and a snake leaped out.

A monk who preached to some nuns accepted a few handkerchiefs from them and tucked them into his habit. When he came home, the abbot asked, “How cometh it to pass, brother, that sin is entered into your bosom?” Another time a young monk, the son of a great man, stood holding the candle while the abbot ate his supper, and a proud thought rose in him. He said nothing. Benedict turned to him: “Sign your heart, brother, for what is it that you say? Sign your heart.”

Gregory does not make his hero all-knowing. He is careful to add that “the spirit of prophecy doth not always illuminate the minds of the prophets,” and Benedict was no exception. What these stories show is an abbot who watched over his monks closely enough to catch a lie, a hidden flagon, or a proud thought, and who often corrected them with a single question.

Some of the stories are about bread. In a year of famine in Campania, the monastery came down to its last five loaves. Benedict told the monks, “Indeed, to-day some want there is, but to-morrow you shall have plenty.” The next morning two hundred bushels of meal lay in sacks before his cell door. Who brought them, and how, Gregory says, “is unknown to this very day.”

In the same hard times Benedict had given away the monastery’s wealth to the poor, until only a little oil in a glass was left. When a subdeacon named Agapitus asked for it, Benedict ordered it given to him. Gregory goes on to tell how a glass of oil was thrown from a window and did not break, and how a barrel in the abbey then filled until the oil ran over. Another time an honest man came to the abbey in trouble because he owed twelve shillings. Benedict did not have so much money, so he prayed for two days. On the third day thirteen shillings were found lying on the chest where the monastery kept its corn, one more than the debt. Gregory had that story from Peregrinus, one of Benedict’s own disciples.

The sick and the troubled came too. Gregory heard from an honourable man named Anthony how a boy of his father’s household was cured of leprosy. A man who had been poisoned was healed at Benedict’s touch, by an abbot who had twice been the target of poison himself. A clergyman of Aquinum, possessed by an evil spirit, had been taken to the shrines of the martyrs, and none of them healed him, “to the end that the world might know what great grace was in the servant of God, Bennet.” Benedict freed him and laid two conditions on him: never to eat meat, and never to seek higher orders. After many years he took orders anyway, and the old torment returned and stayed with him until he died.

The devil, in these stories, is never far away, and sometimes he is faintly ridiculous. Benedict once met him in the likeness of a physician, riding a mule and carrying a horn and a mortar, on his way to the monks “to give them a drench.” Before long one of the old monks was in his grip, and Benedict set him free.

Sometimes, Gregory says, the abbot was present where he was not. When Benedict sent monks to found a monastery at Terracina, the new abbot and his prior both saw him in their sleep, showing them how the buildings should be laid out. When they spoke to him about it afterward, he answered with a question of his own: “Did not I appear to either of you in your sleep, and appointed how and where every place was to be builded?”

Stories like these traveled far beyond the mountain, and they reached the Goths.

A King in Borrowed Shoes

Not every Goth who came to Cassino came to pray. Gregory tells of a cruel Goth named Zalla (Galla in the old English), who had a prisoner bound with cords. When Benedict looked at the bound man, the cords fell away, and Gregory marvels at a man who, “sitting still, did appease the fury of that cruel Goth.”

“In the time of the Goths,” as Gregory puts it, Totila was their king, and Italy was at war. He had heard that the abbot of Cassino had the spirit of prophecy, and he decided to test it. He stopped some way off and sent word that he was coming. Then he dressed his guardsman Riggo in the king’s own shoes and royal robes, gave him three attendants, Vultericus, Rudericus, and Blindinus, and a train of courtiers, and sent him to the abbey as though he were Totila himself.

Benedict was sitting a little way off. When Riggo came within hearing, the abbot called out to him: “Put off, my good son, put off that apparel, for that which thou hast on, is none of thine.” Riggo fell flat on the ground, and so did everyone with him. They did not dare go nearer. They went straight back to the king and told him how quickly they had been found out.

Then Totila came himself. When he saw Benedict sitting some way off, he did not dare come nearer, and he fell to the ground. Benedict asked him two or three times to rise, and at last went to him and lifted him up with his own hands. Then the abbot spoke to the king:

“Much wickedness do you daily commit, and many great sins have you done: now at length give over your sinful life. Into the city of Rome shall you enter, and over the sea shall you pass: nine years shall you reign, and in the tenth shall you leave this mortal life.”

— Benedict to Totila, king of the Goths, in Gregory, Dialogues II, chapter 15 (English of 1608)

From that day, Gregory writes, Totila “was nothing so cruel as before.” And it all came to pass. Totila entered Rome, crossed the sea to Sicily, and in the tenth year of his reign lost his kingdom and his life. Gregory, writing half a century later, knew how the story ended, and he told it as a prophecy fulfilled.

Another visitor, the bishop of Canosa, told Benedict that Totila would leave Rome empty of people. Benedict disagreed: “Rome shall not be utterly destroyed by strangers: but shall be so shaken with tempests, lightnings, whirlwinds, and earthquakes, that it will fall to decay of itself.” Gregory, writing in Rome, needed no proof of that: “we see before our eyes in this very city.” He is honest about his evidence even here. Honoratus, who reported the saying, had it from monks who heard it, not from Benedict himself.

One prophecy Benedict made in tears. A man named Theoprobus, whom Benedict’s counsel had converted and who knew him well, came into his cell one day and found him weeping bitterly. When Theoprobus asked why, Benedict told him:

“All this Abbey which I have built … are by the judgment of almighty God delivered to the gentiles, to be spoiled and overthrown: and scarce could I obtain of God to have their lives spared, that should then live in it.”

— Benedict to Theoprobus, in Gregory, Dialogues II, chapter 17 (English of 1608)

He had built it all, and he could not save it. He had begged to have the lives of his monks spared, and he had barely obtained even that. It happened as he said. Some decades after his death the Lombards came to Monte Cassino by night, while the monks slept, and plundered the abbey. They did not take a single monk. Gregory wrote that the prophecy was “proved most true.”

Benedict’s disciples carried his memory to Rome: Valentinian, for one, had charge of the Lateran abbey there. In 593, three years after he became pope, Gregory the Great sat down, at the request of monks of his household, to gather the wonders of the fathers of Italy, and he gave a whole book to Benedict. He wrote in hard years, with the Lombards in Italy, for people who needed comfort and courage. And he named the men he had his story from:

“All the notable things and acts of his life I could not learn; but those few, which I mind now to report, I had by the relation of four of his disciples: to wit, of Constantinus, a most rare and reverent man, who was next Abbot after him; of Valentinianus, who many years had the charge of the Lateran Abbey; of Simplicius, who was the third General of his order; and lastly of Honoratus, who is now Abbot of that monastery in which he first began his holy life.”

— Gregory the Great, Dialogues II, prologue (English of 1608)

Gregory filled his book with wonders. But when he wanted to show Peter where the real Benedict could be found, he pointed somewhere else. Benedict, he said, “wrote a rule for his monks, both excellent for discretion and also eloquent for the style.” Anyone who wanted to know how he lived could find it there, because he could not teach otherwise than he lived.

A Little Rule for Beginners

The Rule survives, and it is the one place where Benedict speaks to us without Gregory standing between. Gregory gives no date for it, and the sources do not say at what point in his life Benedict wrote it. Its first word is Obsculta: Listen.

“Listen, my son, to the master’s teaching, and turn the ear of your heart. Gladly welcome the advice of a loving father and carry it out, so that you return by the work of obedience to the One you left through the laziness of disobedience.”

— Benedict, Rule, Prologue (our translation from the Latin)

It opens in the voice of a father speaking to a son. The whole of the monk’s life, as Benedict describes it, is a road home: obedience undoing, one day at a time, the old refusal that led away from God. “We must therefore set up a school of the Lord’s service,” he writes, dominici scola servitii. And then the man whose first monks had poisoned his wine sooner than live under his discipline wrote this: “In laying this down we hope to order nothing harsh or heavy.” If something seems a little strict, he goes on, do not run in fear from the way of salvation; “it cannot begin except with a narrow gate.” But the way does not stay narrow. “As life and faith advance, the heart widens, and one runs the way of God’s commands in the unspeakable sweetness of love.”

The fourth chapter lists what Benedict calls the tools of good works, seventy-odd short commands. It begins with the two great commandments, to love God with the whole heart, soul, and strength, and the neighbor as oneself. It runs through the works of mercy: “Refresh the poor. Clothe the naked. Visit the sick. Bury the dead. Help in trouble. Comfort the grieving.” Among them stand four Latin words that the Rule will repeat, almost exactly, near its end: Nihil amori Christi præponere, put nothing before the love of Christ. The list ends with the tool for the days when all the others fail: “And never despair of God’s mercy.”

Where is all this work to be done? “The workshop where we do all this carefully,” Benedict writes, “is the monastery enclosure and stability in the community.” It is a striking demand from this man. Benedict himself had twice walked away from a community, once from monks who tried to kill him and once to spare his young monks from Florentius, and Gregory had to defend him for it. Yet his Rule asks the monk to stay, and on the fourth step of humility it describes a man who, in hard and unjust treatment, “quietly embraces patience in his heart, endures, and does not grow weary or leave.”

That ladder of humility fills the Rule’s seventh chapter. “We must raise the ladder that Jacob saw in his dream,” Benedict writes, and our life in this world is that ladder, with body and soul as its two sides. It has twelve steps. The first is to keep the fear of God always before one’s eyes and never forget it. The last leads somewhere fear cannot go. At the top, he promises, the monk “will come to that love of God which, being perfect, casts out fear.” From then on he will keep every rule “no longer from dread of hell, but from love of Christ, from good habit, and from delight in virtue.”

Then there are the guests. Benedict had been found in his cave by a priest with an Easter dinner and by shepherds, and visited on his mountain by a king in borrowed shoes. He gave a whole chapter of the Rule to visitors, and it begins:

“Let all guests who arrive be received as Christ, because he will say: I was a stranger and you took me in.”

— Benedict, Rule, chapter 53 (our translation from the Latin)

When guests arrive, the brothers bow their heads or lie stretched on the ground before them: “let Christ be adored in them, for Christ is who is received.” The abbot himself pours water over the guests’ hands, and “the abbot and the whole community wash the feet of all guests.” Poor people and pilgrims are to be welcomed with the greatest care of all, “because in them Christ is received more; for the rich, fear itself wins them honour.” And because guests arrive at all hours, the abbot and the guests have a kitchen of their own, so that the brothers are not disturbed by visitors, “who are never lacking in a monastery.” The dryness of that last phrase is pure Benedict.

He brings the same eye to the monastery’s storeroom. The cellarer, the monk who keeps its goods, must be wise and sober, “not a big eater,” and “a father to the whole community.” He must treat all the tools and goods of the monastery “as if they were the sacred vessels of the altar.” The abbot who once fished a Goth’s billhook out of a lake wrote that. He cares “with full attention for the sick, the children, the guests, and the poor,” knowing that he will give account for every one of them on the day of judgment. If he has nothing to give, “let him give a kind word,” and the reason follows: “let no one be troubled or saddened in the house of God.” It is the same voice that told the Goth to be sad no more.

Twice the Rule asks that all things be done with measure, omnia mensurate. It knows people. On wine it sighs: “We read that wine is not for monks at all,” Benedict admits; “but since monks of our times cannot be persuaded of that, let us agree at least not to drink to fullness.” A measure called a hemina each day is enough, he decides, thinking of the weakness of the sick. The care of the sick, he writes, comes before everything else, because Christ is served in them. Of the abbot he asks the hardest thing of all: “let him try to be loved more than feared,” and let him know that he must serve more than rule. When a newcomer knocks, the test is a single question, whether he seeks God in earnest, si revera Deum quaerit.

Work matters, too. “Idleness is the enemy of the soul,” the Rule warns. Monks are monks indeed, it says, when they live by the work of their hands, as the fathers and apostles did, and the day is divided among prayer, work, and sacred reading. The motto most often hung on his name, Ora et labora, pray and work, appears nowhere in the Rule. Terence Kardong, quoted by Subiaco Abbey, traces it to a nineteenth-century book by a German abbot, Maurus Wolter. Paul VI’s letter on Benedict uses the words all the same, as a saying about him.

Near the end, Benedict turns from the abbot and the cellarer to the brothers themselves. There is a bitter zeal, he writes, that separates from God and leads to hell, and a good zeal that separates from vice and leads to God and eternal life. This is how he describes the good zeal:

“Let them try to outdo each other in honour. Let them bear each other’s weaknesses of body and of character with great patience. Let them race one another in obedience. Let no one follow what he thinks useful for himself, but what is useful for the other.”

— Benedict, Rule, chapter 72 (our translation from the Latin)

A rule can tell a monk to be home before nightfall. It cannot tell him what to do when love asks him to stay. Late in his life, Benedict learned that from his sister.

The Storm His Sister Asked For

First, though, Gregory tells of a day when Benedict was asked for something he did not want to give. He was coming home from work in the fields with his monks when a countryman met him. The man had laid the body of his dead son at the abbey gate and run to find the abbot, and when he saw him he cried out, “Give me my son, give me my son!” Benedict drew back:

“Away, my good brethren, away: such miracles are not for us to work, but for the blessed Apostles: why will you lay such a burthen upon me, as my weakness cannot bear?”

— Benedict at the monastery gate, in Gregory, Dialogues II, chapter 32 (English of 1608)

Then he went to the child. He stretched himself over the small body and prayed: “Behold not, O Lord, my sins, but the faith of this man.” The child began to tremble. Benedict gave him back to his father, alive and well. Gregory is careful to say that this wonder came by prayer. Some things, he explains, Benedict did by power and some by prayer, and this one he asked for.

The next story Gregory tells is about a time when Benedict wanted something and did not get it. In Gregory’s words, “he would have had that thing, which yet he could not.”

Benedict had a sister, Scholastica, “dedicated from her infancy to our Lord.” Once a year she came to see him, and he went out with his monks to meet her at a house that belonged to the abbey, not far from the gate. They spent the day “in the praises of God and spiritual talk.” When night came on, they were still at table, and she begged him to stay until morning. He refused. He would not, Gregory says, “by any means tarry all night out of his Abbey.”

The sky was clear. Scholastica folded her hands on the table, laid her head on them, and prayed, weeping. At the moment she lifted her head, thunder broke over the house and the rain came down. Gregory has a phrase for it: “she lifted up her head and brought down the rain.” Benedict, the lawgiver, the man who knew what happened far away and read hidden thoughts, could only say, “God forgive you, what have you done?” His sister answered him:

“I desired you to stay, and you would not hear me, I have desired our good Lord, and he hath vouchsafed to grant my petition: wherefore if you can now depart, a God’s name return to your monastery, and leave me here alone.”

— Scholastica to Benedict, in Gregory, Dialogues II, chapter 33 (English of 1608)

He could not depart. So the brother and sister spent the whole night awake, talking together of the things of God. Gregory’s judgment on the contest is one of the loveliest sentences in his book. Benedict had the rule on his side, and Scholastica had the stronger prayer, and the reason was simple: “she did more which loved more.”

Three days later Benedict was standing in his cell when he saw his sister’s soul leave her body and rise into heaven “in the likeness of a dove.” He sent monks to bring her body to the monastery and had it laid in the grave he had prepared for himself. Gregory explains why: “as their souls were always one in God whiles they lived, so their bodies continued together after their death.”

The Whole World in a Ray

Among the friends who came to Monte Cassino was Servandus, a deacon and the abbot of a monastery in Campania founded by Liberius. Once, during one of his visits, Benedict rested at the top of a tower, with Servandus lodged at its foot and one stair serving them both. Before the night office, Benedict rose, stood at the window, and prayed.

In the dead of night, a light came, far brighter than daylight. Then, as Benedict himself told it afterward, the whole world seemed to be gathered together under a single ray of the sun and set before his eyes. In that light he saw the soul of Germanus, bishop of Capua, carried up to heaven by angels in a globe of fire.

He called out to Servandus two or three times. Servandus came, and saw only “a little remnant of the light.” Benedict told him all that he had seen, and sent word to Theoprobus at Cassino to dispatch a messenger to Capua that night. The messenger learned that Germanus had died at that very hour.

When Peter asked how such a thing could be, Gregory answered with words the Middle Ages remembered: “all creatures be as it were nothing to that soul which beholdeth the Creator.” The young man who had left Rome had gone looking for God alone in a cave. Late in his life, at a tower window, he was shown the whole world at once, gathered in God’s light. He had not lost the world by leaving it.

His own end was near now, and he knew it.

Standing, With Hands Raised

In the year he died, Benedict told some of his monks the day of his death. Those who were with him he told to keep it secret; to those who were far away he gave a sign by which they would know. Six days before the end, he had his grave opened, the grave where Scholastica already lay. Then a fever took hold of him.

On the sixth day he had his disciples carry him into the oratory, and there he received the Body and Blood of Christ. He was too weak to stand, and he stood:

“Having his weak body holden up betwixt the hands of his disciples, he stood with his own lifted up to heaven, and as he was in that manner praying, he gave up the ghost.”

— Gregory the Great, Dialogues II, chapter 37 (English of 1608)

The man who went into a cave to be alone with God died on his feet, at prayer, held up by the hands of his monks.

Two monks, one in his cell and the other far away, saw the same vision that day. A road ran from Benedict’s cell eastward up to heaven, hung with woven cloth and bright with lamps beyond number. A man at the top told them whose road it was: “This is the way by which the beloved servant of God, Bennet, is ascended up to heaven.”

They buried him in the oratory of St. John the Baptist, beside his sister, on the ground where Apollo’s altar had stood when he first came up the mountain. And Gregory adds that the cave at Subiaco, where he had first lived alone, “even to this very time, worketh miracles”: only lately, he writes, a woman out of her mind had slept in that cave and come out healed.

Cross, Book, and Plough

His abbey did not long outlive him. A few decades after his death the Lombards plundered Monte Cassino, as he had foreseen, and the monks escaped with their lives to Rome. The abbey was refounded in the eighth century, sacked by Saracens late in the ninth, and rose again. In France, the monks of Fleury on the Loire came to claim that his bones had been carried to them from the ruined abbey; the claim is first reported in the ninth century, and Monte Cassino disputes it.

On 15 February 1944, Allied bombers destroyed the abbey, and some 230 civilians died there. Three years later, on 21 March 1947, Pope Pius XII wrote that practically nothing had survived the destruction except the crypt where Benedict’s relics are kept. When the ruins were cleared, archaeologists found traces of the two oratories Gregory had described more than thirteen centuries earlier, St. Martin’s and St. John’s, with pre-Christian cellars beneath them.

The abbey was rebuilt. On 24 October 1964 Pope Paul VI consecrated its new church, and on the same day he declared Benedict principal patron of all Europe. Cardinals, bishops, heads of religious orders, and lay leaders from many parts of Europe had asked for it. Pius XII had already called him the father of Europe, and had hoped that Benedict’s prayer would bless those who work to bind the nations of Europe together; John XXIII had shared that hope. Paul VI’s letter, which begins with the words Pacis nuntius, messenger of peace, gathers Benedict’s work into three Latin words: cruce, libro, aratro, by the cross, the book, and the plough. In the East, too, he is remembered: the Orthodox commemorate him on 14 March, and their synaxarion points to Gregory’s book for his life and says that he “raised the dead, foretold the future.”

Many people first meet Benedict on a small medal. On one side he holds a cross and his Rule, with a cup beside him and a raven with a loaf. The English of Gregory used here says crow, and the cup and the loaf were two separate attacks by two different enemies, but the medal joins them. On the other side, letters run around a cross. They stand for Latin verses: May the sacred cross be my light; let not the dragon be my guide; step back, Satan, never urge vain things on me; what you offer is evil, drink the poison yourself.

The verses are medieval, and for a while even their meaning was lost. In 1647, at a witchcraft trial at Natternberg in Bavaria, the accused said they had no power over the nearby abbey of Metten, because the abbey was protected by the cross. The monks of Metten found crosses painted on their walls with these letters, and no one remembered what they meant. The answer turned up in a manuscript of 1415 at the abbey, which showed Benedict holding a staff topped with a cross and a scroll, with the words written out in full. Pope Benedict XIV approved the medal in 1741 and 1742.

For all these honors, the Rule itself does not sound like the work of a man who expected to be called the father of Europe. In its last chapter, Benedict calls it hanc minimam inchoationis regulam, this least little rule for beginners.

He had gone into a cave to be alone with God, and God kept sending him people: a monk with a rope, a priest with a dinner, shepherds, nobles’ sons, a Goth, a king, a sister. He died standing, held up by their hands. And in the little rule he left them, the chapter on how brothers should love one another ends with a line about where they are going. Let them put absolutely nothing before Christ, “who will lead us all together to eternal life.”

A Note on the Sources

Almost everything known of Benedict’s life comes from one book, the second book of Gregory the Great’s Dialogues, written in 593 or 594, some fifty years after Benedict’s death, from the memories of four named disciples and a few others. Gregory gives no dates at all. The usual dates are later inferences: a birth about 480, the founding of Monte Cassino about 529, and Totila’s visit in 543, the one date the Catholic Encyclopedia of 1907 calls certain. Gardner places Totila’s visit probably in 542. For the death, the Catholic Encyclopedia gives 543, Gardner (as “the tradition”) and Guérin give 21 March 543, the 1911 Britannica gives about 544, and popular modern references, such as Wikipedia, give 547; the sources do not agree. Gregory wrote to strengthen faith, and the historian F. Homes Dudden (1905) read many of his stories as legends that grew quickly in an age that expected wonders, calling the Cassino years “dimly discernible through a haze of legend.” A few scholars, from Huldreich Coccius in 1551 to Francis Clark in the 1980s, have doubted that Gregory wrote the Dialogues at all. Paul Meyvaert answered Clark in defense of Gregory’s authorship. We know this debate only from abstracts and titles, and the older sources used here treat the book as Gregory’s.

Later tradition added things Gregory does not say. It named Benedict’s parents and made Scholastica his twin, a tradition the Catholic Encyclopedia says Bede accepted. It said he died on Holy Saturday, which, Guérin notes, does not fit the date of Easter in 543, and that Maurus carried the Rule to Gaul. Gregory does not name the monastery of the poisoned cup; Vicovaro is a later identification. Chapter numbers for Gregory follow the Latin division into 38 chapters; Luck’s 1880 printing of the 1608 English divides the book into 48. Quotations from the Rule are cited by chapter, because most verse numbers could not be confirmed.

How This Life Was Researched

This life was written from 25 sources in English, Latin, and French. Its core is Gregory the Great’s Dialogues, Book II, the only early life, read in the English translation of 1608 in three printings. Beside it stands Benedict’s Rule, read in Latin and checked against Oswald Hunter Blair’s English of 1907. The researchers copied 25 passages of the Rule and 21 passages of Gregory for quotation, and the English of the Rule quoted here is our own. Two papal documents were read at the Vatican’s site: Pius XII’s encyclical of 1947 and Paul VI’s apostolic letter of 1964, the latter only in Latin. Dudden’s study of Gregory (1905), Gardner’s notes (1911), the Catholic Encyclopedia, the 1911 Britannica, Guérin’s French Petits Bollandistes, Ullathorne (1860), and two older accounts of the Benedict medal supplied the later record. Several sources were not read: the Latin text of Gregory’s Dialogues, Paul the Deacon, the Regula Magistri debate, and the work of Meyvaert and de Vogüé. Nor were the English translations of the Rule by McCann (1952) and Verheyen (1949), Bede, or the English text of Pacis nuntius.

saint.relic_description:
Gregory the Great writes that Benedict was buried in the oratory of St. John the Baptist at Monte Cassino, in the grave where he had laid his sister Scholastica. When Allied bombing destroyed the abbey in February 1944, Pope Pius XII wrote in 1947 that practically nothing survived except the crypt where the relics are kept. A 2025 New Liturgical Movement article reports that the relics of Benedict and Scholastica lie under the high altar of the rebuilt church, and that the effigy tombs in the crypt are cenotaphs.

The claim is contested. From the ninth century the abbey of Fleury (Saint-Benoît-sur-Loire, France) has said that its monks carried the relics there after the Lombards ruined Monte Cassino; Monte Cassino disputes it. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1907) records the doubt and notes that Abbot Tosti decided for Monte Cassino. According to Wikipedia, Fleury’s reliquary was melted down by Protestant troops in the Wars of Religion.
saint.relic_location: Abbey of Monte Cassino, Italy (claim contested by Fleury Abbey, Saint-Benoît-sur-Loire, France)

miracles.miracles:
This list gathers the wonders told of St. Benedict of Nursia, with their sources and their status. Nearly all of them come from one book: the second book of the Dialogues of Pope Gregory the Great, written in 593 or 594, about fifty years after Benedict’s death, from the accounts of four named disciples (Constantine, Valentinian, Simplicius, and Honoratus) and a few other witnesses whom Gregory names story by story. Benedict was honored as a saint long before the Church had formal procedures for canonization, and no source we read shows any of these accounts being examined or approved in a canonical process. The list makes no claim of scientific proof, and it does not dismiss any account. Chapter numbers follow the Latin division of Gregory’s book into 38 chapters; where it is known, the number in Luck’s 1880 printing of the 1608 English, which divides the book into 48, is given too. The old English calls Benedict “Bennet.”

During Benedict’s life

The broken sieve at Effide

When the young Benedict left Rome, his nurse went with him to Effide (the old English “Enside,” modern Affile). She borrowed a sieve from the neighbors, and it fell and broke in two. Benedict gathered the pieces and “with tears fell to his prayers,” and found the sieve “so whole that the place could not be seen where before it was broken.” The townspeople hung it over the door of their church, where Gregory says it still hung “even to these very troubles of the Lombards.”

Status: recorded by Gregory the Great from Benedict’s disciples. No formal Church approval.

Source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues II, ch. 1 (ch. 3 in Luck), Gardner ed., 1911.

A priest sent to the cave on Easter Day

While Benedict lived hidden in a cave at Subiaco, a priest far away who had prepared a good dinner heard the Lord say to him in a vision: “Thou hast provided good cheer for thyself, and my servant in such a place is afflicted with hunger.” The priest went out and found Benedict in his cave on Easter Day. Benedict had not known it was Easter.

Status: recorded by Gregory. No formal Church approval.

Source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues II, ch. 1 (ch. 6 in Luck), Gardner ed., 1911.

The poisoned glass shatters

The monks of a neighboring monastery, whose abbot had died, persuaded Benedict to rule them, then resented his discipline and mixed poison into his wine. When he made the sign of the cross over the glass, it broke in pieces “as though the sign of the cross had been a stone thrown against it.” Benedict asked God to forgive them, told them to seek another father, and returned to the wilderness. Gregory does not name the monastery; later tradition identifies it with Vicovaro. This is a different attack from the poisoned loaf below.

Status: recorded by Gregory. No formal Church approval. The cup appears on the St. Benedict Medal.

Source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues II, ch. 3 (ch. 9 in Luck), Gardner ed., 1911.

The monk who could not stay at prayer

In one of the Subiaco monasteries, whose father was Pompeianus, a monk could never stay at prayer and kept wandering out. Benedict saw what Gregory describes as a little black boy, a demon, drawing the monk out by the skirt of his habit. No one else could see it until Maurus did, after two days. Benedict struck the monk with a wand, and from then on he stayed at prayer.

Status: recorded by Gregory. No formal Church approval.

Source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues II, ch. 4, Gardner ed., 1911.

Water from the mountain rock

Three of Benedict’s monasteries stood on a mountain without water, and the monks were worn out carrying it. One night Benedict climbed the mountain with the boy Placidus, prayed, and laid three stones on the spot. The next day the monks dug where the stones lay; the rock began “sweating drops of water,” and a spring flowed that Gregory says ran “even to this day.” Peter, in the dialogue, compares it to Moses striking the rock.

Status: recorded by Gregory. No formal Church approval.

Source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues II, ch. 5 (ch. 12 in Luck), Gardner ed., 1911.

The Goth’s billhook rises from the lake

A Goth, poor in spirit, who had joined the community was clearing briers by the lake at Subiaco when the iron head of his billhook slipped off into water “so deep, that there was no hope.” Benedict put the empty handle into the lake, and the iron rose from the bottom. “Behold here is thy bill again,” he said, “work on, and be sad no more.” Peter, in the dialogue, compares it to Elisha’s axe-head. This Goth is not the debtor of the twelve shillings below.

Status: recorded by Gregory. No formal Church approval.

Source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues II, ch. 6 (ch. 13 in Luck), Gardner ed., 1911.

Maurus runs on the water to save Placidus

The boy Placidus fell into the lake, and the water carried him out “so far as one may shoot an arrow.” Benedict, in his cell, knew it at once and sent Maurus, who ran across the surface of the water and pulled Placidus out by the hair. Benedict credited Maurus’s obedience; Maurus credited the abbot’s command. Placidus said he had seen “the Abbot’s garment upon his head” as he was drawn out.

Status: recorded by Gregory. No formal Church approval.

Source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues II, ch. 7 (ch. 14 in Luck), Gardner ed., 1911.

The crow and the poisoned loaf

Florentius, the priest of a nearby church and grandfather of a subdeacon Gregory knew, envied Benedict and sent him a poisoned loaf. Benedict told the crow that came every day from the nearby wood to take bread from his hand: “In the name of Jesus Christ our Lord, take up that loaf, and leave it in some such place where no man may find it.” The crow hopped about and cried, and at last “with much ado” carried the loaf away, returning three hours later for its usual bread. The 1608 English says crow; the St. Benedict Medal shows a raven. Florentius later died when the room where he was collapsed, and Benedict mourned him and gave Maurus a penance for rejoicing at the news.

Status: recorded by Gregory. No formal Church approval. The bird and loaf appear on the St. Benedict Medal.

Source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues II, ch. 8 (chs. 15–17 in Luck), Gardner ed., 1911.

“Blessed Bennet” and “Cursed Bennet”

After Benedict destroyed the shrine of Apollo on the mountain at Cassino and built oratories of St. Martin and St. John the Baptist in its place, Gregory says the devil appeared to him visibly. The monks saw nothing but heard the voice call “Blessed Bennet,” and then, “Cursed Bennet, and not blessed: what hast thou to do with me?”

Status: recorded by Gregory. No formal Church approval.

Source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues II, ch. 8, Gardner ed., 1911.

The stone that would not move

While Monte Cassino was being built, a stone the monks needed could not be moved, because the monks decided the devil was sitting on it. When Benedict blessed it, it could be moved.

Status: recorded by Gregory. No formal Church approval.

Source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues II, ch. 9 (ch. 19 in Luck), Gardner ed., 1911.

The phantom fire in the kitchen

When the monks dug up an idol of brass, the kitchen seemed to burst into flames. The fire was only a phantom.

Status: recorded by Gregory. No formal Church approval.

Source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues II, ch. 10 (ch. 20 in Luck), Gardner ed., 1911.

A young monk crushed by a falling wall

The devil, Gregory says, threw down a new wall at Monte Cassino, and it fell on a young monk, the son of a courtier. His bones were so broken that he was carried to Benedict in a sack. Benedict prayed alone in his cell, and in the same hour the young monk was sound and went back to work on the wall. This is a wall, not a tower; the tower in Gregory’s book is where Benedict later saw the vision of the whole world.

Status: recorded by Gregory. No formal Church approval.

Source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues II, ch. 11 (ch. 21 in Luck), Gardner ed., 1911.

Monks who ate outside the monastery

Some monks ate at the house of a devout woman, against the rule of the house, and denied it on their return. Benedict named the house, the food, and the number of cups: “Why do you tell an untruth?”

Status: recorded by Gregory. No formal Church approval.

Source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues II, ch. 12 (ch. 22 in Luck), Gardner ed., 1911.

Valentinian’s brother eats on the road

The brother of Valentinian, one of Gregory’s four witnesses, was a layman who would not eat on his way to the abbey until he arrived. Once he ate on the road, and Benedict told him so when he came.

Status: recorded by Gregory. No formal Church approval.

Source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues II, ch. 13 (ch. 23 in Luck), Gardner ed., 1911.

Riggo in the king’s clothes

Totila, king of the Goths, tested Benedict’s gift of prophecy by sending his guardsman Riggo in the royal shoes and robes, with three attendants, Vultericus, Rudericus, and Blindinus. From a little way off Benedict called: “Put off, my good son, put off that apparel, for that which thou hast on, is none of thine.” Riggo and his escort fell to the ground and went back to the king. The 1907 Catholic Encyclopedia dates the visit to 543; Gardner (1911) says probably 542.

Status: recorded by Gregory. No formal Church approval.

Source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues II, ch. 14 (ch. 24 in Luck), Gardner ed., 1911.

The prophecy to Totila

When Totila came in person and lay on the ground before him, Benedict raised him and told him: “Into the city of Rome shall you enter, and over the sea shall you pass: nine years shall you reign, and in the tenth shall you leave this mortal life.” Gregory, writing about fifty years later, says Totila entered Rome, crossed to Sicily, and lost kingdom and life in his tenth year, and that he was “nothing so cruel as before.”

Status: a prophecy recorded by Gregory, who tells its fulfilment. No formal Church approval.

Source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues II, ch. 15 (ch. 25 in Luck), Gardner ed., 1911.

Rome will decay of itself

The bishop of Canosa told Benedict that Totila would leave Rome uninhabited. Benedict answered: “Rome shall not be utterly destroyed by strangers: but shall be so shaken with tempests, lightnings, whirlwinds, and earthquakes, that it will fall to decay of itself.” Gregory says he saw this “before our eyes in this very city.” Honoratus, who reported the saying, had it from monks who heard it, not from Benedict himself.

Status: a prophecy recorded by Gregory at second hand. No formal Church approval.

Source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues II, ch. 15, Gardner ed., 1911.

The possessed clergyman of Aquinum

A clergyman of Aquinum, possessed by an evil spirit, had been taken to martyrs’ shrines without being healed, “to the end that the world might know what great grace was in the servant of God, Bennet.” Benedict freed him and forbade him to eat meat or to take higher orders. After many years he took orders, and he died possessed.

Status: recorded by Gregory. No formal Church approval.

Source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues II, ch. 16 (ch. 26 in Luck), Gardner ed., 1911.

The sack of Monte Cassino foretold

Theoprobus, a convert who knew Benedict well, found Benedict weeping bitterly in his cell. Benedict told him that the whole abbey would be “delivered to the gentiles, to be spoiled and overthrown,” and that “scarce could I obtain of God to have their lives spared.” Gregory reports that the Lombards later sacked the abbey by night while the monks slept, and not one monk was taken. Gardner dates the sack to 589; other sources give earlier dates.

Status: a prophecy recorded by Gregory, who tells its fulfilment. No formal Church approval.

Source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues II, ch. 17 (ch. 27 in Luck), Gardner ed., 1911.

The snake in the hidden flagon

Exhilaratus, a lay brother whom Gregory’s listener knew, hid a flagon of wine in a bush. Benedict warned him: “Take heed, my son, that thou drinkest not of that flagon which thou hast hidden in the bush: but first be careful to bow it down, and thou shalt find what is within it.” When he tipped it over, a snake leaped out.

Status: recorded by Gregory. No formal Church approval.

Source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues II, ch. 18 (ch. 28 in Luck), Gardner ed., 1911.

The handkerchiefs

A monk who preached to some nuns accepted handkerchiefs from them and hid them in his habit. Benedict asked him on his return: “How cometh it to pass, brother, that sin is entered into your bosom?”

Status: recorded by Gregory. No formal Church approval.

Source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues II, ch. 19 (ch. 29 in Luck), Gardner ed., 1911.

The proud thought of the candle-bearer

A young monk, the son of a great man, was holding a candle for Benedict when a proud thought rose in him. He said nothing, but Benedict told him: “Sign your heart, brother, for what is it that you say? Sign your heart.”

Status: recorded by Gregory. No formal Church approval.

Source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues II, ch. 20 (ch. 30 in Luck), Gardner ed., 1911.

Two hundred bushels of meal in a famine

During a famine in Campania, the monastery was down to five loaves. Benedict said, “Indeed, to-day some want there is, but to-morrow you shall have plenty.” The next day two hundred bushels of meal were found at the monastery door; who brought them, Gregory says, “is unknown to this very day.”

Status: recorded by Gregory. No formal Church approval.

Source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues II, ch. 21 (ch. 31 in Luck), Gardner ed., 1911.

The dream plan for Terracina

When Benedict sent monks to found a monastery at Terracina, the abbot and the prior both saw him in their sleep, showing them where the buildings should go. Later he asked them: “Did not I appear to either of you in your sleep, and appointed how and where every place was to be builded?”

Status: recorded by Gregory. No formal Church approval.

Source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues II, ch. 22 (ch. 32 in Luck), Gardner ed., 1911.

Nuns absolved after their death

Two nuns of noble family lived near the abbey and could not curb their tongues, and they often provoked the good man who served them. Benedict sent word that he would excommunicate them unless they amended, and they did not. After they died and were buried in the church, the nurse who made an offering for them saw them rise from their graves and leave whenever the deacon told those who did not communicate to depart. When Benedict was told, he gave an offering with his own hands: “Go your ways, and cause this to be offered unto our Lord for them, and they shall not remain any longer excommunicate.” After it was offered, they were not seen to leave again.

Status: recorded by Gregory. No formal Church approval.

Source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues II, ch. 23 (ch. 33 in Luck), Gardner ed., 1911.

The boy cast out of his grave

A young monk who loved his parents more than reason went to their house without asking Benedict’s blessing, and died the same day. When he was buried, his body was found cast out of the grave the next day, and again the day after. His family went to Benedict in tears. He gave them the Communion of the Lord’s body: “Go, and lay with great reverence this our Lord’s body upon his breast, and so bury him.” After that the body lay quietly in the grave.

Status: recorded by Gregory. No formal Church approval.

Source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues II, ch. 24 (ch. 34 in Luck), Gardner ed., 1911.

The dragon

A monk so restless that he kept asking to leave was at last told by Benedict, wearied by his pleading, to go. He was no sooner out of the abbey gate than he met a dragon in the way with its mouth open, and he cried out, “Help, help! for this dragon will eat me up.” The monks who ran out saw no dragon, but found him shaking and brought him back, and he promised never to leave again.

Status: recorded by Gregory. No formal Church approval.

Source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues II, ch. 25 (ch. 35 in Luck), Gardner ed., 1911.

A leper boy healed

Gregory heard from Anthony, “honourable man,” that a boy of his father’s household was cured of leprosy by Benedict.

Status: recorded by Gregory from a named informant. No formal Church approval.

Source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues II, ch. 26 (ch. 36 in Luck), Gardner ed., 1911.

Twelve shillings owed, thirteen found

An honest man who owed twelve shillings (Latin solidi) came to Benedict for help. Benedict did not have so much money and prayed for two days. On the third day thirteen shillings were found on the chest where the monastery kept its corn. Gregory had the story from Peregrinus, one of Benedict’s disciples. The debtor is not a Goth; the Goth of the lost billhook is a different man.

Status: recorded by Gregory from a named informant. No formal Church approval.

Source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues II, ch. 27 (ch. 37 in Luck), Gardner ed., 1911.

A poisoned man healed by a touch

A man who had been poisoned was healed when Benedict touched him.

Status: recorded by Gregory. No formal Church approval.

Source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues II, ch. 27 (ch. 38 in Luck), Gardner ed., 1911.

The glass of oil and the overflowing barrel

In a time of famine Benedict ordered that the little oil the monastery had left be given to the subdeacon Agapitus. A glass of oil thrown from a window did not break, and afterward a barrel in the abbey filled until the oil overflowed.

Status: recorded by Gregory. No formal Church approval.

Source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues II, chs. 28–29 (ch. 39 in Luck), Gardner ed., 1911.

The devil dressed as a doctor

Benedict saw the devil disguised as a physician, riding a mule with a horn and a mortar, going to the monks “to give them a drench.” An old monk was afflicted, and Benedict freed him. Here Gregory notes that Benedict did some wonders by power and some by prayer.

Status: recorded by Gregory. No formal Church approval.

Source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues II, ch. 30 (ch. 40 in Luck), Gardner ed., 1911.

Zalla’s prisoner set free by a look

A cruel Goth named Zalla (Galla in the 1608 English) had a prisoner bound with cords. When Benedict looked at the bound man, the cords fell away. Gregory admires a man who, “sitting still, did appease the fury of that cruel Goth.”

Status: recorded by Gregory. No formal Church approval.

Source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues II, ch. 31 (ch. 41 in Luck), Gardner ed., 1911.

A dead child restored to his father

A countryman laid his dead son at the monastery gate and cried to Benedict, returning from the fields, “Give me my son, give me my son!” Benedict first refused: “such miracles are not for us to work, but for the blessed Apostles.” Then he stretched himself over the child and prayed, “Behold not, O Lord, my sins, but the faith of this man.” The child trembled, revived, and was given back to his father alive and well. Gregory says this came by prayer.

Status: recorded by Gregory. No formal Church approval.

Source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues II, ch. 32 (ch. 42 in Luck), Gardner ed., 1911.

Scholastica’s storm

On her yearly visit, Benedict’s sister Scholastica begged him to stay the night, and he refused to spend a night outside his abbey. Under a clear sky she laid her head on her folded hands and prayed in tears; as she lifted her head, thunder and rain broke, and he could not leave. “I desired you to stay, and you would not hear me,” she told him, “I have desired our good Lord, and he hath vouchsafed to grant my petition.” They talked all night. Gregory: “she did more which loved more.”

Status: recorded by Gregory. No formal Church approval. Gregory gives no year; tradition gives 10 February 543 for her death.

Source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues II, ch. 33 (ch. 43 in Luck), Gardner ed., 1911.

Scholastica’s soul seen as a dove

Three days later, standing in his cell, Benedict saw his sister’s soul rise to heaven “in the likeness of a dove.” He had her body laid in the grave he had prepared for himself.

Status: a vision recorded by Gregory. No formal Church approval.

Source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues II, ch. 34 (ch. 44 in Luck), Gardner ed., 1911.

The whole world in one ray of light

While the abbot Servandus was visiting, Benedict rose before the night office and prayed at a window of the tower where they slept. A light brighter than day came in the night, and, as Benedict later told it, the whole world seemed gathered together under a single ray of the sun before his eyes. He saw the soul of Germanus, bishop of Capua, carried to heaven by angels in a globe of fire. Servandus, called, saw only “a little remnant of the light,” and a messenger sent to Capua found that Germanus had died at that hour.

Status: a vision recorded by Gregory, from Benedict’s own account. No formal Church approval. Whether Benedict saw God himself in it was later debated by theologians.

Source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues II, ch. 35 (ch. 45 in Luck), Gardner ed., 1911.

His death foretold, and the road of lamps

In the year of his death Benedict told his monks the day; six days before, he had his grave opened. On the sixth day of a fever he received Communion in the oratory and died standing, held up by his disciples, with his hands raised in prayer. Two monks, one in his cell and one far away, saw the same vision: a road hung with tapestry and lit with lamps, running east from his cell to heaven, and a man who said, “This is the way by which the beloved servant of God, Bennet, is ascended up to heaven.”

Status: recorded by Gregory. No formal Church approval. Gregory gives no year, month, or day; the death year is given as 543, about 544, or 547 in different sources.

Source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues II, ch. 37 (ch. 47 in Luck), Gardner ed., 1911.

After Benedict’s death

A woman healed in his cave at Subiaco

Gregory writes that the cave at Subiaco where Benedict first lived “even to this very time, worketh miracles, if the faith of them that pray requireth.” He tells of a woman out of her mind who had lately slept in the cave and was healed.

Status: recorded by Gregory, writing about fifty years after Benedict’s death. No formal Church approval.

Source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues II, chs. 37–38 (chs. 47–48 in Luck), Gardner ed., 1911.

The miracles recorded at Fleury

The abbey of Fleury on the Loire in France claimed from the ninth century that it held Benedict’s relics, carried from the ruined Monte Cassino; Monte Cassino disputes the claim. Monks of Fleury, among them Andrew of Fleury around 1043, compiled a collection called the Miracula S. Benedicti. Its accounts were not read for this entry.

Status: a medieval collection of a contested shrine. No formal Church approval.

Source: “Fleury Abbey,” Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fleury_Abbey; “St. Benedict of Nursia,” Catholic Encyclopedia, 1907, New Advent.

The cross at Metten, 1647

At a witchcraft trial at Natternberg in Bavaria in 1647, the accused said they had no power over the nearby abbey of Metten because it was protected by the cross. The monks found crosses with mysterious letters painted on their walls; a manuscript of 1415 at Metten showed Benedict with a cross-staff and a scroll, with the words written out in full. This led to the St. Benedict Medal, approved by Pope Benedict XIV in 1741 and 1742. The verses on the medal are medieval, not Benedict’s own.

Status: popular devotion and a reported protection, not a miracle examined by the Church. The medal itself is an approved sacramental.

Source: Michael Ott, “Medal of Saint Benedict,” Catholic Encyclopedia, 1912, New Advent; Prosper Guéranger, The Medal or Cross of St. Benedict, 1880, Internet Archive.

teachings.teachings:
Benedict left one writing: his Rule for monks. Gregory the Great, the only early witness to his life, says he “wrote a rule for his monks, both excellent for discretion and also eloquent for the style,” and that anyone who wants to know how Benedict lived can find it there, because he could not teach otherwise than he lived. No source gives the date or place of writing. The themes below are a doorway into it. The English is our own translation from the Latin, checked against Oswald Hunter Blair’s 1907 translation; passages are cited by chapter, because most verse numbers could not be confirmed. The motto Ora et labora (pray and work) is not in the Rule.

Listen with the ear of the heart

The Rule begins with one word, Obsculta: Listen. Benedict speaks as a father to a son, and he describes the monk’s life as a way home: obedience, freely given, undoes the old disobedience that led away from God.

“Listen, my son, to the master’s teaching, and turn the ear of your heart. Gladly welcome the advice of a loving father and carry it out, so that you return by the work of obedience to the One you left through the laziness of disobedience.”

— Benedict, Rule, Prologue (our translation)

These are the opening lines of the Rule, written for men entering his monasteries. Benedict had listened himself when he was young: he left his studies, his father’s house, and its wealth in Rome to seek God at Subiaco.

Nothing before the love of Christ

Everything in the Rule serves one center: Christ, loved above all. Benedict says it twice, once among the “tools of good works” in chapter 4 and again in the last line of chapter 72, where he adds that Christ leads the whole community together to eternal life.

“Let them put absolutely nothing before Christ, who will lead us all together to eternal life.”

— Benedict, Rule, 72:11 (our translation)

The shorter form in chapter 4 is four Latin words, Nihil amori Christi præponere, “Put nothing before the love of Christ” (4:21). Benedict lived it from his youth: Gregory says he left his books and his inheritance, and at the end he died standing in the oratory, having received the Body and Blood of Christ, with his hands raised in prayer.

A school with nothing harsh or heavy

Benedict calls the monastery a school, where people learn to serve God. He hopes to lay down nothing harsh, and he promises that the narrow beginning widens into joy.

“As life and faith advance, the heart widens, and one runs the way of God’s commands in the unspeakable sweetness of love.”

— Benedict, Rule, Prologue (our translation)

Just before, he writes: “We must therefore set up a school of the Lord’s service” (Prologue 45), and “In laying this down we hope to order nothing harsh or heavy.” The man who wrote this had been an abbot whose first monks tried to poison him because they could not bear his discipline and who then founded new communities at Subiaco and at Cassino.

The tools of good works

Chapter 4 lists more than seventy short commands that Benedict calls tools. They begin with love of God and neighbor and run through the works of mercy.

“Refresh the poor. Clothe the naked. Visit the sick. Bury the dead. Help in trouble. Comfort the grieving.”

— Benedict, Rule, chapter 4 (our translation)

The list includes a warning against vanity: “Do not wish to be called holy before you are. First be what can truly be said.” It ends with the tool for the worst days: “And never despair of God’s mercy.” The workshop for all of them is “the monastery enclosure and stability in the community.” Gregory shows Benedict praying with tears over his nurse’s broken sieve and in sorrow over a countryman’s dead son, and refusing credit when Maurus walked on the water.

The ladder of humility

In chapter 7 Benedict takes Jacob’s ladder as a picture of the monk’s life: body and soul are its two sides, and there are twelve steps of humility. The first is to keep the fear of God always in view. The last is love.

“When all the steps are climbed, the monk will come to that love of God which, being perfect, casts out fear. He will keep all things no longer from dread of hell, but from love of Christ, from good habit, and from delight in virtue.”

— Benedict, Rule, chapter 7 (our translation)

On the fourth step, the monk in hard and unjust treatment “quietly embraces patience in his heart, endures, and does not grow weary or leave.” Benedict answered the monks who poisoned him “with a mild countenance and quiet mind,” and mourned the priest who had tried to poison him when he died.

Every guest received as Christ

Hospitality is one of the Rule’s great themes. Guests are received as Christ himself, the poor and pilgrims most of all, the abbot pours water over their hands, and the whole community washes their feet.

“Let all guests who arrive be received as Christ, because he will say: I was a stranger and you took me in.”

— Benedict, Rule, chapter 53 (our translation)

The same chapter gives the poor a special place, “because in them Christ is received more; for the rich, fear itself wins them honour,” and gives the guests a separate kitchen, since guests “are never lacking in a monastery.” Benedict called a priest’s visit to his cave on Easter Day his feast, and he raised a Gothic king who lay on the ground before him.

Tools as altar vessels, and a kind word

In chapter 31 the cellarer, who keeps the monastery’s goods, must be “a father to the whole community.” Ordinary things are to be treated with reverence, and people with gentleness.

“Let him treat all the tools and goods of the monastery as if they were the sacred vessels of the altar.”

— Benedict, Rule, chapter 31 (our translation)

If he has nothing to give, “let him give a kind word,” so that “no one be troubled or saddened in the house of God.” Gregory tells how Benedict brought a Goth’s lost billhook up from the bottom of a lake and handed it back: “work on, and be sad no more.”

Measure in all things

Benedict asks for measure, omnia mensurate, and allows for human weakness, often with dry humor.

“We read that wine is not for monks at all, but since monks of our times cannot be persuaded of that, let us agree at least not to drink to fullness.”

— Benedict, Rule, chapter 40 (our translation)

He sets a hemina of wine a day, thinking of the weakness of the sick, and puts the care of the sick “before all and above all.” Gregory, who called the Rule “excellent for discretion,” shows the same balance in the man: strict about his own rule, yet overruled by his sister’s prayer.

Work, prayer, and sacred reading

The Rule divides the monk’s day among prayer, work, and sacred reading. Work has its own place beside prayer.

“Idleness is the enemy of the soul.”

— Benedict, Rule, chapter 48 (our translation of Otiositas inimica est animæ)

The same chapter says monks are such when they live by the work of their hands, as the fathers and apostles did. The motto Ora et labora is not in the Rule; Terence Kardong, quoted by Subiaco Abbey, traces it to a nineteenth-century book by Abbot Maurus Wolter. In Gregory’s stories Benedict comes in from work in the fields, and sends a monk healed of his injuries straight back to work on the wall.

An abbot loved more than feared

Benedict asks the abbot to lead by serving.

“Let him try to be loved more than feared.”

— Benedict, Rule, chapter 64 (our translation of et studeat plus amari quam timeri)

In the same chapter he tells the abbot that he must serve more than rule, prodesse magis quam præesse. Gregory shows him correcting monks with a question (“Sign your heart, brother”) and giving away the monastery’s last oil in a famine.

The good zeal

Near the end of the Rule, Benedict sets a bitter zeal that leads away from God against a good zeal that leads to God, and describes the good zeal as life together.

“Let them try to outdo each other in honour. Let them bear each other’s weaknesses of body and of character with great patience. Let them race one another in obedience. Let no one follow what he thinks useful for himself, but what is useful for the other.”

— Benedict, Rule, chapter 72 (our translation)

Benedict calls the whole Rule, in its last chapter, “this least little rule for beginners,” hanc minimam inchoationis regulam. He died held up by the hands of his monks.

gaps: Length: the biography has about 7,760 words by the lint count, below the tier A target of 8,000–10,000. Gregory’s Dialogues II is the only early life, and every scene the notes support is told; the rest would be padding.
Lint: no MUST FIX lines; the remaining CHECK lines are long narrative sentences, kept for rhythm.

Death year conflict: Gregory gives no date. The Catholic Encyclopedia gives 543; Gardner (as “the tradition”) and Guérin give 21 March 543; Britannica 1911 gives c. 544; Wikipedia and popular sources give 547 (not verified). Gardner puts Totila’s visit probably in 542; the Catholic Encyclopedia and Britannica say 543. death_year and birth_year (c. 480, inference) are left null.
Feast days come from Wikipedia (11 July, Roman calendar since 1969; 21 March before) and, for 14 March, also from Sanidopoulos’s synaxarion; not checked in a Roman or Orthodox calendar text.
Unverified and left out of the text: canonization by Honorius III in 1220 and co-patronage of Europe in 1980 (Wikipedia only).
Pacis nuntius was read only in Latin; the English of its phrases is our own.
Rule verse numbers: only Prol. 45, 4:21, and 72:11 are confirmed (Benedict XVI, 2008); all other Rule passages are cited by chapter.
The “whole world under one beam of the sun” wording came from garbled OCR and is paraphrased, not quoted.

Gregory chapters 23–25 (nuns absolved, boy cast from his grave, dragon) were outlined by the researchers only. The checker read them in the 1608 text (Gardner 1911) and the miracles list now tells them.
Totila’s scene follows Gregory’s words: Benedict, “speaking to him twice or thrice,” asked him to rise and then lifted him up. The earlier draft said “three times”; fixed.

Not read: McCann 1952, Verheyen 1949, the Latin of Gregory, Paul the Deacon, the Regula Magistri debate, Meyvaert and de Vogüé in full, Bede, Adrevald and the Miracula S. Benedicti, the English text of Pacis nuntius.

Clark’s authorship doubt and Meyvaert’s reply are known only from titles and abstracts; the biography states Clark’s doubt without a date for the supposed forgery, and does not claim how most scholars now judge it. Adalbert de Vogüé is not named on authorship because no source read confirms his position.
The Latin of Gregory was not read, so the crow-or-raven question rests on the 1608 English (crow) and the medal (raven); the biography does not say what the Latin word means.
